events.title: Early Settlement
events.description: Archaeological evidence shows human activity on Hispaniola island (where Haiti is located) around 5000 BCE. These early inhabitants were likely hunter-gatherers who migrated from Central or South America. They used stone tools and settled along coasts and rivers. Archaeological sites have been discovered throughout Haiti, including cave paintings and early pottery fragments.

events.title: Pre-Ceramic Culture
events.description: Early inhabitants of Hispaniola developed complex hunter-gatherer societies. They exploited the island's abundant marine and forest resources. Sites from this period show advances in stone tool manufacturing, including polished stone axes and fishing implements. These early inhabitants established seasonal camps, following food sources in migrations.

events.title: Arawak Arrival
events.description: Arawakan-speaking peoples began migrating from the Orinoco River basin of South America to Caribbean islands. They traveled across oceans in canoes, bringing agricultural techniques, pottery making and more advanced tools. The Arawaks cultivated cassava (manioc), corn, sweet potatoes and other crops. They established permanent villages and developed more complex social structures.

events.title: Aristide's First Term
events.description: Aristide inaugurated February 7, 1991 (fifth anniversary of Duvalier's fall). His brief term attempted implementing reforms: raising minimum wage; fighting smuggling and corruption; beginning military and police reform; promoting literacy and public health projects; negotiating with US and international financial institutions. However, Aristide faced powerful opposition: military threatened by his plans to cut army and hold accountable for human rights violations; elite opposed economic reforms and empowering poor; Aristide's inflammatory rhetoric (calling for 'necklacing' punishment for corrupt elite with burning tires) was controversial; US uncomfortable with Aristide's populism and anti-American rhetoric. After just seven months, military launched coup.

events.title: Massive Slave Uprising Erupts
events.description: Slaves on Northern Plain launched massive uprising, marking formal beginning of Haitian Revolution. Thousands of slaves attacked plantations, killing white planters and overseers, burning cane fields and buildings. Boukman led rebel army, flames illuminated night sky, smoke shrouded Northern Plain. Within days, hundreds of plantations destroyed, about 1,000 whites killed, about 100,000 slaves joined uprising. Colony descended into chaos and terror. White colonists retreated to defend towns, appealing to France for help. Uprising's violence shocked entire Atlantic world, slaveholders in Europe and Americas felt fear. This was largest slave uprising in modern history, that would change world history's course.

events.title: Saladoid Culture
events.description: Saladoid culture, an Arawak branch, established prosperous agricultural societies on Hispaniola. They were known for their fine white-on-red painted pottery decorated with geometric patterns and animal figures. Saladoid people developed complex village systems, constructing round or oval thatched houses. Their society had initial class stratification and religious rituals.

events.title: Ostionoid Culture
events.description: Ostionoid culture emerged in the Caribbean region, replacing Saladoid culture. Societies in this period were more complex, village sizes expanded, with more pronounced social hierarchies. Pottery styles changed, with decoration becoming simpler. Agricultural techniques improved and populations grew. This culture laid foundation for later Taíno culture.

events.title: Taíno Culture Formation
events.description: Taíno culture matured on Hispaniola and surrounding islands. The Taínos were an Arawakan-speaking people who established complex chiefdom societies. Taínos developed sophisticated agricultural systems including conuco fields, cultivating cassava, corn, beans, peanuts, peppers, pineapples and tobacco. They invented the hammock (hamaca) and canoe (canoa), words that later entered European languages.

events.title: Taíno Civilization at its Peak
events.description: Taíno civilization reached its zenith. Hispaniola (called Ayiti or Quisqueya in Taíno, meaning 'mountainous land') had an estimated population of hundreds of thousands to over a million. The island was divided into five major chiefdoms (cacicazgos), each ruled by a paramount chief (cacique). Taíno society had clear classes: nobles (nitaínos), commoners (naborias) and caciques. They built large ceremonial plazas (bateys) for ball games (similar to soccer) and religious ceremonies. Taínos practiced polytheistic religion, worshipping ancestors and nature spirits (cemíes). They created fine wood carvings, stone sculptures and golden ornaments. Taínos developed complex systems of agriculture, fishing and trade networks, maintaining connections with other Caribbean islands. Their society was relatively peaceful, though occasional conflicts occurred with Caribs from Lesser Antilles.

events.title: Columbus' First Landing
events.description: Christopher Columbus arrived at Hispaniola island during his first transatlantic voyage, the second large island he discovered in New World (first was Cuba). He named the island 'La Isla Española' (Spanish Island), later evolving to Hispaniola. Columbus landed near Môle Saint-Nicolas, receiving friendly welcome from Taínos. Cacique Guacanagarix offered gifts and assistance. Columbus was very interested in island gold, and gold ornaments worn by Taínos convinced Spaniards the island had rich gold mines.

events.title: Santa María Shipwreck and La Navidad
events.description: Columbus' flagship Santa María ran aground and sank on Hispaniola's north coast. Cacique Guacanagarix sent hundreds to help salvage cargo and equipment. Using shipwreck timber, Columbus built first European settlement—La Navidad (meaning 'Christmas')—leaving 39 Spanish men. This was first European permanent (though brief) colonial outpost in Americas. Columbus then sailed back to Spain aboard Niña, bringing gold samples and Taíno captives to report New World discovery to Spanish monarchs.

events.title: Columbus' Second Voyage and La Navidad Destruction
events.description: Columbus returned to Hispaniola with 17 ships and about 1,200 colonists for large-scale colonization. When he returned to La Navidad, he found the fort destroyed and all 39 Spaniards dead. According to Taínos, these Spaniards became greedy and brutal after Columbus left, robbing gold and raping women, eventually triggering Taíno resistance. Warriors led by Cacique Caonabo attacked and destroyed La Navidad. This marked the beginning of violent conflict between Taínos and Spanish colonizers, foreshadowing decades of bloody conquest.

events.title: La Isabela Established
events.description: Columbus established first formal colonial city—La Isabela—on island's north coast, named after Spanish Queen Isabella I. This was first European city in Americas, with church, governor's palace, warehouses and residences. About 1,500 colonists settled there. However, due to poor site selection (malaria and other diseases rampant), food shortages, Taíno resistance and less gold than expected, La Isabela faced serious difficulties. Conflicts and rebellions erupted among colonists. Columbus forced to impose harsh measures to maintain order, inflicting cruel punishments on both colonists and Taínos.

events.title: Gold Tribute System
events.description: Columbus established cruel tribute system. All Taínos over 14 had to deliver fixed amount of gold dust every three months (in mining areas) or 25 pounds of cotton (in other areas). Taínos who completed tribute received copper token to wear around neck as proof. Those who failed had hands cut off or were executed. This system was extremely brutal, as island's gold reserves were far less than Spanish expected, many Taínos forced to pan gold day and night in rivers, causing agricultural abandonment, famine and death. Many Taínos committed suicide or fled to mountains to escape this system.

events.title: Wars of Conquest
events.description: Spanish launched full military conquest against resisting Taínos. Columbus and his brother Bartholomew led about 200 Spanish soldiers, 20 horses and 20 hunting dogs (specially trained to attack humans) to suppress Taínos. Despite Taínos' large numbers (tens of thousands of warriors), their weapons (wooden clubs, stone axes, bows and arrows) couldn't match Spanish steel swords, firearms, cavalry and ferocious war dogs. Taínos suffered devastating defeats in several decisive battles. Thousands of Taínos killed, thousands enslaved. Cacique Caonabo captured and sent to Spain (died en route). This war marked end of organized Taíno resistance and consolidation of Spanish rule on island.

events.title: Nueva Isabela (Santo Domingo) Established
events.description: Due to La Isabela's difficulties, Columbus' brother Bartholomew established new city—Nueva Isabela—on island's south coast, later renamed Santo Domingo. This city had excellent location with good harbor, quickly becoming capital and main base for Spanish colonial enterprise in Americas. Santo Domingo is oldest continuously inhabited European city in Americas, later becoming Spanish springboard for expansion into Mexico, Central and South America. City developed rapidly, constructing Americas' first church, first hospital, first university and first stone buildings.

events.title: Columbus Arrested
events.description: Due to colonial mismanagement, colonists' complaints and reports of brutal rule, Spanish Crown sent investigator Francisco de Bobadilla to Hispaniola. Bobadilla arrested Columbus and his brothers, sent them back to Spain in chains for trial. Though Columbus later released and partially restored to honor, he lost governorship of colony. This marked Spanish Crown's beginning of direct control over New World colonies, no longer relying on individual explorers. Though freed, Columbus never regained power in Hispaniola.

events.title: Governor Nicolás de Ovando
events.description: Nicolás de Ovando appointed governor of Hispaniola, arriving with 2,500 colonists—largest fleet to New World at that time. Ovando reorganized colonial administration, establishing organized government in Santo Domingo. His policies toward Taínos more systematized but equally brutal. Ovando established encomienda system, allocating Taínos to Spanish colonists as labor force. Nominally, Spaniards were to protect and Christianize Taínos, but in practice this was disguised slavery. Taínos forced to labor in gold mines, plantations and construction sites under extremely harsh conditions.

events.title: Xaragua Massacre
events.description: In Xaragua region, local female cacica Anacaona invited Governor Ovando to peaceful feast, trying to improve relations with Spanish. It was a trap. Ovando's troops suddenly attacked, killing assembled Taíno nobles and warriors. Anacaona captured and later hanged. Estimated hundreds of Taíno leaders killed in this event. Many Taíno commoners massacred or enslaved. Xaragua Massacre was one of most infamous events of Spanish systematic genocide against Taínos, completely destroying Taíno power structure in that region.

events.title: Enriquillo Rebellion Begins
events.description: Taíno cacique Enriquillo led last major Taíno uprising. Enriquillo raised in Spanish monastery, spoke Spanish, received Catholic education. But when his wife was raped by a Spaniard, he appealed to Spanish authorities and was ignored, so he led followers to flee into Baoruco Mountains (today's southwestern Haiti) launching guerrilla war. Enriquillo's rebels used mountain terrain, successfully resisting Spanish forces for over a decade. They raided Spanish plantations and settlements, liberating enslaved Taínos. Enriquillo's rebellion became symbol of Taíno resistance.

events.title: Diego Columbus Governor
events.description: Christopher Columbus' son Diego Columbus appointed governor of Hispaniola, partially restoring Columbus family position in colony. Diego built magnificent governor's palace (Alcázar de Colón) in Santo Domingo, this Renaissance-style building still exists today, oldest viceregal palace in Americas. Under his rule, colony continued expanding, but exploitation of Taínos also intensified. Encomienda system further consolidated, Taíno population plummeted due to overwork, disease and starvation.

events.title: Taíno Population Collapse
events.description: Taíno population experienced catastrophic collapse. When Columbus arrived in 1492, Hispaniola estimated to have 300,000 to 1 million Taínos. By 1510s, population reduced to about 60,000. By 1520s, only thousands remained. Population collapse had multiple causes: European diseases (smallpox, measles, influenza) devastated Taínos with no immunity; overwork and abuse under encomienda system caused massive deaths; famine (due to destruction of Taíno agricultural systems); violent suppression and massacres; despair-induced low birth rates and suicide. This was one of fastest and most thorough population extinctions in human history.

events.title: Montesinos' Denunciation
events.description: Dominican friar Antonio de Montesinos delivered famous sermon in Santo Domingo, publicly denouncing Spanish colonists' cruel treatment of Taínos. He questioned colonists: 'Are these Indians not men? Do they not have rational souls?' This sermon shocked colony, sparking intense debate about colonial ethics and indigenous rights. Montesinos' protest reached Spain, prompting Spanish Crown to review colonial policies. This event influenced Bartolomé de Las Casas—a colonist who became greatest defender of Indian rights.

events.title: Laws of Burgos
events.description: In response to criticism of colonist abuses, Spanish Crown promulgated Laws of Burgos, first laws regulating Spanish-indigenous relations. Laws prescribed certain limits on encomienda system, requiring colonists to provide food, shelter and religious instruction to indigenous people, prohibiting certain most cruel abuses. However, these laws rarely enforced in practice, lacking effective oversight mechanisms, and colonists and local officials often ignored them. Laws actually legitimized encomienda system, Taínos' situation did not substantially improve.

events.title: First African Slaves
events.description: As Taíno population collapsed, severe labor shortage emerged. Spanish colonists began importing slaves from Africa to replace Taíno workers. First African slaves arrived directly from Africa to Hispaniola. Initially small numbers, but quickly grew massively. African slaves considered more capable of enduring harsh labor and European diseases than Taínos (as Africans had some immunity to certain diseases). This marked beginning of transatlantic slave trade in Americas—a trade that would transport about 12 million Africans to Americas over next three centuries, becoming one of largest forced migrations in human history.

events.title: Sugar Industry Begins
events.description: As gold mine resources depleted, Hispaniola's economy shifted toward agriculture, especially sugarcane cultivation. First sugar mills (ingenios) established, using water or ox-powered mills to process sugarcane. Sugar industry required massive labor, further driving African slave imports. However, Hispaniola's sugar industry remained relatively limited in this period, as Spanish attention and resources shifted to newly discovered, wealthier territories—Mexico (conquered by Cortés in 1519) and Peru (conquered by Pizarro in 1530s). Many colonists left Hispaniola for these new conquests seeking fortune.

events.title: Enriquillo Peace Treaty
events.description: After over a decade of guerrilla warfare, Spanish authorities finally reached peace agreement with Enriquillo. Spanish realized they couldn't militarily defeat Enriquillo, so proposed negotiations. Treaty recognized freedom of Enriquillo and his followers, granted them land, and pardoned past 'crimes.' Enriquillo given title 'Don,' becoming legitimate figure in Spanish colonial system. Though personal victory for Enriquillo, Taínos as a people were already near extinction. Enriquillo's rebellion became legend of Caribbean resistance to colonial oppression, he himself became symbol of freedom and resistance, honored as national hero in both modern Haiti and Dominican Republic.

events.title: Hispaniola's Decline
events.description: Hispaniola's status as center of Spanish colonial enterprise dramatically declined. Mexico and Peru's silver mines and larger indigenous populations attracted most Spanish attention and immigration. Island's gold depleted, population reduced, economy stagnant. Santo Domingo remained important administrative center and transshipment port, but its relative importance greatly diminished. Colonist population decreased, many towns abandoned. Island's western and northern regions especially deserted, Spanish control concentrated in south and east. This neglect created conditions for later French penetration in island's west.

events.title: Pirates and Smuggling
events.description: Hispaniola's sparsely populated northern and western coasts became haven for pirates, privateers and smugglers from France, England and Holland. Pirates attacked Spanish ships and coastal towns. Island colonists engaged in lucrative smuggling trade with these 'invaders,' as Spain's monopoly trade policies restricted legal trade. Wild cattle and pigs (introduced from Europe then gone feral) bred in island's west, attracting hunters including French 'buccaneers' (boucaniers)—named for their use of boucan (smoking rack) to make dried meat. These buccaneers gradually established permanent settlements in island's west.

events.title: Forced Relocation Policy
events.description: To combat smuggling and piracy, Spanish Governor Antonio Osorio implemented radical 'devastation policy' (devastaciones). He ordered evacuation of all Spanish towns in northern and western coasts (including Bayajá, Yaguana, Montecristi and Puerto Plata), forcibly relocating residents to inland areas near Santo Domingo. Purpose was to cut smugglers' supply sources and eliminate pirates' sanctuaries. This policy was disastrous: many colonists died during relocation, massive livestock slaughtered, economy devastated. Worse, policy backfired—abandoned northern and western regions opened doors for foreign penetration, especially French.

events.title: French Occupation of Tortuga
events.description: French pirates and settlers occupied Tortuga island off Hispaniola's north coast. This small island became famous pirate base and France's first Caribbean foothold. Tortuga's French pirates (including buccaneers and filibusters, i.e. pirates) attacked Spanish ships and towns, accumulating massive wealth. Spanish repeatedly tried to recapture Tortuga, but French always returned. From Tortuga, French began penetrating Hispaniola's western mainland, establishing plantations and settlements. This marked beginning of France's long-term presence in region, eventually leading to island's division.

events.title: French Expansion in West
events.description: French settlers gradually moved from Tortuga to Hispaniola's west. They were initially hunters and small farmers, but gradually began cultivating tobacco, indigo and other crops. French presence in west became increasingly solid, despite Spain claiming sovereignty over entire island. French government began more actively supporting these settlers, sending governors and troops. Small-scale conflicts occurred between Spain and France on island, but Spain unable to expel French as its resources concentrated on protecting more valuable colonies. French settlers imported more African slaves to develop plantation economy.

events.title: Plantation Economy Development
events.description: French-controlled west (not yet formally named) saw plantation economy rapidly develop. French colonists established large sugarcane, coffee, indigo and cotton plantations. These plantations completely depended on African slave labor. Slave trade dramatically increased, tens of thousands of Africans transported to island. Plantation system was extremely brutal: slaves worked 16-18 hours daily in scorching heat, subjected to harsh punishments, with poor food and housing conditions. Death rates were extremely high, many slaves died within years, requiring constant African imports to replenish labor force. This 'sugar mill' economy brought massive profits to France, but was built on horrifying human suffering.

events.title: Treaty of Ryswick
events.description: Treaty of Ryswick ended Nine Years' War (War of Grand Alliance), one clause was Spain formally recognizing French sovereignty over Hispaniola's western third. French colony was called Saint-Domingue, while Spanish part retained original name Santo Domingo. Treaty did not clearly define borders, leading to continued border disputes. This division sowed seeds for modern Haiti and Dominican Republic's separation. Saint-Domingue quickly surpassed Spanish part in prosperity, becoming France's most valuable colony. Santo Domingo city (Spanish part's capital) relatively declined, with population and economy far behind French part.

events.title: Saint-Domingue Prosperity
events.description: Saint-Domingue became one of world's wealthiest colonies in 18th century, called 'Pearl of the Antilles.' Colony produced 40% of world's sugar and 60% of coffee, plus massive amounts of indigo, cotton, cocoa and other tropical crops. Port-au-Prince (became capital in 1770) and Cap-Français (today's Cap-Haïtien) became bustling trade ports. French merchants, planters and officials accumulated enormous wealth. Colony's exports exceeded total of all thirteen British North American colonies. However, this prosperity was entirely built on slavery, with about 500,000 African slaves laboring under extremely brutal conditions.

events.title: Makandal Maroon Rebellion
events.description: A maroon (escaped slave) named Makandal led resistance movement. Makandal reportedly from Guinea, was vodou priest and strategist. After losing an arm in plantation accident, he escaped to mountains, organizing network of maroons. Makandal planned massive uprising, targeting all whites by poisoning water supplies and food. Over six years, thousands of whites allegedly died from poisoning (though actual numbers may be exaggerated). Makandal captured in 1758, burned alive in Cap-Français square. But his legend lived among slaves, foreshadowing later great revolution. Many slaves believed Makandal did not die, but escaped by transforming into a mosquito.

events.title: Port-au-Prince Becomes Capital
events.description: Port-au-Prince replaced Cap-Français as Saint-Domingue's capital. Port-au-Prince on Gulf of Gonâve had excellent harbor, more centrally located. City developed rapidly, constructing magnificent buildings, theaters and squares. Port-au-Prince became colony's administrative, commercial and cultural center. City attracted French colonists, free colored elite and foreign merchants. However, city also built on slave labor: slaves worked in city as domestic servants, artisans and dock workers. Port-au-Prince's luxury contrasted sharply with plantation slaves' misery.

events.title: Enlightenment Ideas and Abolitionism
events.description: Enlightenment ideas, especially concepts of liberty, equality and human rights, began spreading in Saint-Domingue. Société des Amis des Noirs (Society of Friends of Blacks) founded in France, advocating abolition of slavery or at least improving slave treatment. These ideas influenced some free people of color, many of whom educated in France and exposed to these ideals. However, white planters strongly opposed any reform, as their wealth completely depended on slave labor. Colony social tensions intensified: white planters wanted more autonomy but keeping slavery; free people of color demanded equal rights; slaves yearned for freedom. These contradictions laid foundation for coming revolutionary explosion.

events.title: French Revolution Impact
events.description: News of French Revolution reached Saint-Domingue, causing shock. Declaration of Rights of Man and Citizen proclaimed 'men are born free and equal,' creating huge problem in colony with large slave population. Different groups had different understandings of revolution: white colonists hoped to use revolutionary chaos to gain more autonomy while keeping slavery; free people of color demanded full equality based on human rights principles; slaves began questioning why they couldn't be free. Paris revolutionary government vacillated on colonial policy, sending contradictory signals. Saint-Domingue tensions dramatically escalated, preparing for violent conflict.

events.title: Free People of Color Uprising
events.description: Free colored leaders Vincent Ogé and Jean-Baptiste Chavannes launched armed uprising, demanding French National Assembly grant free people of color equal rights. Uprising brutally suppressed by colonial authorities, Ogé and Chavannes captured and executed on the wheel (bound to wheel with bones broken). This cruel punishment shocked many, intensifying racial tensions. White colonists refused any reform, leading to civil war between free people of color and whites. Meanwhile, slaves closely watched these developments, preparing their own action.

events.title: Bois Caïman Ceremony
events.description: In Bois Caïman forest near Cap-Français, slave leaders held secret vodou ceremony, planning full uprising. Legendarily, vodou priestess Cécile Fatiman presided over ceremony, sacrificing a black pig, participants drank blood and swore to overthrow slavery. Leaders included Dutty Boukman—a slave from Jamaica and vodou priest. Boukman delivered passionate speech declaring: 'Cast away the white god's image, it makes us weep. Listen to freedom's voice in our hearts!' This ceremony became legendary starting point of Haitian Revolution, symbolizing fusion of African spiritual traditions with liberation struggle.

events.title: Uprising Spread and Suppression
events.description: Slave uprising rapidly spread throughout Northern Province. Rebel army established camps and fortifications, showing remarkable organizational ability. Colonial authorities and white militia tried to suppress uprising, both sides engaged in fierce battles. In November, Boukman killed in combat, his head displayed in Cap-Français as warning. But uprising didn't end, new leaders emerged, including Jean-François, Biassou, and a former slave named Toussaint Louverture (born Toussaint Bréda), who would become revolution's greatest leader. Rebel army controlled large rural areas, colonial economy severely damaged.

events.title: Three-Way Civil War
events.description: Saint-Domingue descended into complex three-way civil war: slave rebel army controlled northern countryside; white colonists split into royalists and republicans; free people of color launched their own uprising in south and west, demanding equal rights. France sent troops and new commissioners trying to restore order. Alliances formed and broke between different factions, violence continually escalated. In April, French National Assembly granted free people of color full citizenship, trying to divide rebels. But this enraged white colonists, intensifying civil war. Colonial economy collapsed, trade interrupted, famine spread. Foreign powers (Spain and Britain) began intervening, hoping to profit from chaos or seize colony.

events.title: Cap-Français Burned
events.description: In conflict between whites and free people of color, Cap-Français—colony's wealthiest, most prosperous city—was burned. Thousands of white refugees fled to United States (mainly Philadelphia and Baltimore), bringing stories of slave uprising terror, triggering panic among American slaveholders. City's destruction marked symbolic end of old colonial order. Meanwhile, Britain and Spain invaded Saint-Domingue, trying to use chaos to seize this wealthy colony. France was fighting multiple nations in Europe (French Revolutionary Wars), unable to send sufficient reinforcements to Saint-Domingue, colony faced danger of foreign occupation.

events.title: Slavery Abolition Proclamation
events.description: Facing British and Spanish invasions and risk of losing colonial control, French Commissioner Léger-Félicité Sonthonax made radical decision, proclaiming slavery abolition in Northern Province, promising all former slaves become free French citizens. This was tactical decision, aiming to win rebel army support against foreign invaders. In September and October, abolition decree extended to Western and Southern Provinces. This made Saint-Domingue first European colony to abolish slavery (earlier than France itself). However, actual implementation faced enormous difficulties, many white planters opposed, while former slaves uncertain whether to trust this promise.

events.title: French National Convention Abolishes Slavery
events.description: Paris National Convention approved Saint-Domingue's abolition decree, formally abolishing slavery in all French colonies. Saint-Domingue delegate Jean-Baptiste Belley—a former slave—spoke in Convention supporting abolition. This decision was revolutionary at time, making France first European great power to abolish slavery in its colonial empire (though Napoleon later restored it). Abolition decree changed Saint-Domingue war's nature: former slaves now had reason to support French Republic against British and Spanish invaders trying to restore slavery. This created conditions for Toussaint Louverture to join French side.

events.title: Toussaint Joins France
events.description: Toussaint Louverture previously allied with Spain against France, but after France abolished slavery, he realized France offered best opportunity for achieving black freedom. Toussaint led 4,000 well-trained soldiers to French side. This was war's turning point. Toussaint was exceptional military strategist and leader, he quickly defeated Spanish forces, recovered lost territory. In following years, Toussaint became most important French commander in Saint-Domingue, fighting British invaders. He established disciplined army, implemented land reform, restored economic production. Toussaint's leadership and vision for former slaves made him symbol of black liberation movement.

events.title: Treaty of Basel
events.description: France and Spain signed Treaty of Basel, ending war between two countries. Treaty stipulated Spain cede eastern Hispaniola (Santo Domingo) to France. Though actual transfer not completed until 1801, treaty theoretically unified entire island. Toussaint's army played key role in defeating Spanish. After Spanish withdrawal, war focus shifted to fighting British forces still in colony's south and west. British invasion lasted five years (1793-1798), becoming one of their most costly overseas military operations in history, causing about 40,000 British soldiers' deaths from combat and disease (especially yellow fever).

events.title: British Withdrawal
events.description: After five years of disastrous campaigns, British forces withdrew from Saint-Domingue. Toussaint's military genius, black soldiers' brave fighting, and yellow fever (to which local black soldiers had relatively strong resistance) defeated British. Before withdrawal, British signed secret agreement with Toussaint, recognizing his de facto leadership position in colony. British defeat shocked Europe, proving former slave armies could defeat European great powers' armies. Toussaint now controlled most of Saint-Domingue, though nominally still loyal to France. He began rebuilding economy, forcing former slaves to return to plantation work (as paid laborers not slaves), restoring export production while guaranteeing freedom. This policy was controversial, as many former slaves hoped to own their own small farms rather than work for former masters.

events.title: Complex Racial Hierarchy
events.description: Saint-Domingue developed complex racial and class system. Population divided into three categories: whites (blancs, about 40-50,000)—colony's ruling class including large planters, small planters, merchants and officials; free people of color (gens de couleur libres or affranchis, about 30-40,000)—mainly mixed-race descendants of whites and blacks, some owned property and even slaves, but legally discriminated against; slaves (esclaves, about 500,000)—vast population majority with no rights. Further subdivisions existed within each category. Free people of color were in especially complex position: though some were quite wealthy, laws prohibited them from holding certain positions, marrying whites, wearing certain clothes or using certain names. This discrimination caused free colored resentment, they played key role in revolution.

events.title: Civil War: Toussaint vs Rigaud
events.description: Civil war erupted between Toussaint and southern free colored leader André Rigaud, called 'War of Knives.' This conflict had racial undertones: Toussaint primarily led blacks (former slaves), while Rigaud led mulattoes (free people of color). Both sides claimed to represent Republic, but fought for colonial control. War was extremely brutal, both sides committed atrocities. In 1800 Toussaint's army won, Rigaud fled to France. Toussaint eliminated last major challenge to his authority, now controlled almost all Saint-Domingue. He established highly centralized military government, himself as supreme leader, though still nominally acknowledging French sovereignty.

events.title: Conquest of Spanish Santo Domingo
events.description: Toussaint led army into island's east—former Spanish colony Santo Domingo (today's Dominican Republic). Though Spain ceded it to France in 1795, France never effectively occupied. Toussaint met light resistance and controlled entire island. He abolished slavery still existing in east, liberating about 3,000 slaves. Toussaint now ruled entire Hispaniola, making him de facto independent ruler. He reorganized government, promoting capable black and mulatto officers and officials. Toussaint began being viewed as 'Black Napoleon,' his achievements inspired enslaved and oppressed peoples throughout Atlantic world.

events.title: Toussaint Constitution
events.description: Toussaint promulgated new constitution, declaring himself governor-for-life of Saint-Domingue with power to name successor. Constitution confirmed slavery abolition as permanent and irrevocable, proclaiming 'all men are born free.' Constitution established limited autonomous government, though still nominally acknowledging French sovereignty. Constitution guaranteed religious freedom, promoted commerce, trying to attract foreign merchants and investment. However, constitution also established authoritarian rule, granting Toussaint enormous powers. More importantly, Toussaint unilaterally promulgated constitution without Paris consent, enraging French First Consul Napoleon Bonaparte. Napoleon considered Toussaint overstepping authority, decided to reassert French direct control over colony—and secretly planned to restore slavery.

events.title: Independence War
events.description: After Toussaint's capture, news came that France restored slavery (Napoleon restored it in Guadeloupe in May), Saint-Domingue blacks and mulattoes realized France intended to re-enslave them. Previously surrendered generals—especially Dessalines—relaunched uprising. War became genocidal: French used dogs, hanging and drowning to mass-kill blacks; black armies killed all white French. Both sides committed horrifying atrocities. However, yellow fever decimated French forces, tens of thousands of French soldiers including General Leclerc died. Replacing General Rochambeau was even more brutal, using poison gas and live burial, but couldn't reverse situation. Dessalines-led black armies gradually defeated French. European war resumed in 1803 (Napoleonic Wars), Napoleon couldn't send reinforcements.

events.title: French Expeditionary Force Arrives
events.description: Napoleon sent massive expeditionary force to Saint-Domingue led by his brother-in-law General Charles Leclerc, aiming to restore French direct control, remove Toussaint's power, and secretly restore slavery. Expeditionary force included about 20,000 elite soldiers, Napoleon's largest overseas military operation. In February, French landed at multiple points. Toussaint initially tried negotiating, but quickly realized France intended to eliminate black freedom. War resumed. Toussaint ordered scorched-earth tactics, burning cities and plantations to prevent French using these resources. He issued proclamation: 'Fight for freedom!' Cap-Français and other cities burned. Saint-Domingue again descended into total war.

events.title: Toussaint Captured
events.description: After months of fighting, some of Toussaint's key generals surrendered to France, including Jean-Jacques Dessalines and Henri Christophe. Toussaint became isolated, agreed to negotiate with French. In May, French used negotiations as pretense to trap and arrest Toussaint. He was sent to France in chains. Napoleon imprisoned Toussaint in cold Fort de Joux fortress in Jura Mountains. Toussaint was badly treated there, deprived of adequate food, clothing and medical care. On April 7, 1803, this great liberator died alone in his cell, reportedly from pneumonia and malnutrition. Before capture, Toussaint prophetically wrote: 'In overthrowing me, you have cut down only the trunk of Saint-Domingue freedom tree. It will grow again from roots, for roots are deep and numerous.'

events.title: Battle of Vertières
events.description: At Vertières—a plantation near Cap-Français—occurred independence war's decisive battle. Black armies led by Dessalines and Christophe defeated French last major defensive position in Saint-Domingue. Despite French having better weapons and fortifications, black soldiers charged with remarkable courage, willing to sacrifice to capture French positions. Vertières victory secured independence, France forced to admit defeat. This was one of Napoleon's military career's most devastating defeats, also major victory for abolitionist movement. French remnants evacuated Saint-Domingue, ending over 200 years of French colonial rule on island. Over 50,000 French soldiers died in this war, France lost its most valuable colony.

events.title: Haitian Declaration of Independence
events.description: Jean-Jacques Dessalines declared colonial independence at Gonaïves, restoring Taíno name 'Haiti' (Hayti, meaning 'mountainous land' or 'high land'). Haiti became first independent nation in Latin America, world's first free state founded by former slaves, and first black republic. Independence declaration was radical and filled with anger, condemning French brutality and slavery evils. Declaration proclaimed: 'We must secure our independence with fire and blood...forever renounce France, preferring death to living under its rule.' Dessalines was declared Haiti's governor and commander-in-chief, later self-proclaimed as Emperor Jacques I. Haiti's independence shocked and inspired world: it proved slaves could overthrow masters, establish their own nation. This inspired abolitionist and independence movements throughout Americas, but also caused slaveholding nations' fear, leading to Haiti's international isolation.

events.title: Dessalines Rule and Massacre
events.description: Dessalines established authoritarian rule, self-proclaimed as Emperor Jacques I in September 1804. He tried rebuilding war-destroyed economy, forcing former slaves to work on plantations, though as paid laborers. This caused many peasants' discontent, who hoped to own their own land. In February-April 1804, Dessalines ordered massacre of remaining French whites on island (about 3,000-5,000), as retaliation for French brutality and eliminating 'eternal enemy.' Almost all whites killed, including women and children, only useful professionals like doctors, priests and Polish soldiers (who sympathized with blacks) spared. This atrocity consolidated Haiti's international isolation. Dessalines' dictatorship and brutal rule, plus discrimination against mulatto elite, sparked opposition. On October 17, 1806, Dessalines was ambushed and assassinated en route to suppress rebellion.

events.title: North-South Division
events.description: After Dessalines' death, Haiti split into two rival states: North ruled by Henri Christophe, who self-proclaimed as King Henry I in 1811, establishing Kingdom of Haiti; South led by Alexandre Pétion, establishing republic. This division reflected tensions between black and mulatto elites, plus disagreements about national development direction. Christophe implemented authoritarian modernization in north, forced labor, constructing magnificent buildings (including famous Sans-Souci Palace and Citadelle Laferrière), establishing nobility system, promoting education. Pétion's south was more liberal, distributed land to former soldiers, but economic development slower. Both regimes refused French sovereignty, but faced continued French threats and international isolation. Pétion provided crucial aid to South American liberator Simón Bolívar, on condition Bolívar promised to abolish slavery in areas he liberated.

events.title: Boyer Unifies Haiti
events.description: Pétion died in 1818, Jean-Pierre Boyer succeeded as southern president. Christophe suffered stroke then committed suicide in 1820, north descended into chaos. Boyer seized opportunity, northern nobility surrendered, Boyer unified Haiti in 1820. In 1822, Boyer led army into island's east (former Spanish Santo Domingo, then briefly independent as 'Spanish Haiti'), unifying entire Hispaniola. Boyer abolished slavery in east, but his rule was unpopular with local white and mulatto elites, who resented black leadership and land reform. Boyer's unification marked Haiti's maximum territorial extent, but also sowed seeds for later separation (Dominican independence in 1844).

events.title: French Indemnity
events.description: French King Charles X issued royal decree demanding Haiti pay 150 million francs (later reduced to 90 million) as price for recognizing independence and compensating former colonists' 'losses' (i.e., lost slaves and property). France threatened military invasion, dispatching fleet to blockade Haitian ports. President Boyer agreed to pay under economic and military pressure. This massive indemnity was disastrous: it equaled Haiti's many years of national income, forcing Haiti to borrow from French banks (at high interest). Haiti took over a century to pay off this 'independence debt' (final payment in 1947). This indemnity seriously hindered Haiti's economic development, draining national resources, preventing investment in education, infrastructure and industrial development. Many historians consider this major cause of Haiti's long-term poverty. It was also unjust: Haiti was only nation required to pay for abolishing slavery, actually former slaves paying former masters compensation.

events.title: Boyer's Fall and Dominican Independence
events.description: Boyer's long rule (1818-1843) became increasingly corrupt and unpopular. He forced peasants to work on plantations, suppressed opposition, heavy taxation to pay French indemnity. In 1843, uprising called 'La Réforme' (Reform) overthrew Boyer, he fled abroad. Haiti descended into political instability. On February 27, 1844, eastern island's Spanish-speaking elite seized opportunity to declare independence, establishing Dominican Republic. Haiti attempted multiple military conquests of east, but all failed, finally recognizing Dominican independence in 1856. Losing eastern territory was major setback for Haiti, permanently dividing island into two nations. After Boyer's fall, Haiti entered long period of political turmoil, frequent government changes, economic decline, deepening social divisions.

events.title: Emperor Soulouque
events.description: Faustin-Élie Soulouque from general became president, then self-proclaimed as Emperor Faustin I in 1849. Soulouque was former slave, established court and nobility system imitating Europe, including duke, count titles. He suppressed mulatto elite (many had expected him to be easily manipulated puppet), elevated blacks, promoted vodou. Soulouque repeatedly invaded Dominican Republic, but all failed, consuming massive resources. His rule was lavish but ineffective, economy continued declining, corruption rampant. In 1859, coup overthrew Soulouque, he fled to Jamaica exile. Soulouque era symbolized Haiti's political absurdity and tragedy: a republic founded by former slaves became farcical empire, while nation sank into poverty.

events.title: Period of Political Chaos
events.description: From 1860 to 1915 US occupation, Haiti experienced extreme political instability, with 22 presidents ruling, most overthrown or assassinated. Coups, civil wars and uprisings became norm. This period characterized by: struggles between black and mulatto elites; military (cacos—mainly rural black militias) frequent political intervention; corruption and nepotism; economic stagnation; increasing foreign debt; foreign (especially US, France and Germany) commercial and political intervention increased. Power mainly concentrated in Port-au-Prince elite hands, vast poor peasants marginalized. Education, healthcare and infrastructure extremely inadequate. Haiti's international reputation declined, viewed as failed state. This period consolidated Haiti's status as Western Hemisphere's poorest, most unstable nation.

events.title: US Occupation Period
events.description: US occupation had profound and contradictory impacts on Haiti. Positives: US built roads, bridges, hospitals and schools; improved sanitation and public health; established professional gendarmerie (replacing old army); stabilized finances; eliminated coup cycle. Negatives: occupation was racist and humiliating—during same Jim Crow era in American South, white Marines treated black Haitians as inferior race; US restored corvée forced labor system (similar to slavery) for building roads; US censored press, suppressed political opposition; US military killed thousands of Haitian civilians, especially suppressing cacos uprisings (1918-1920); US changed constitution allowing foreigners to own land; economic benefits mainly flowed to US companies. Occupation deepened Haitian resentment toward US, though some acknowledged certain modernization achievements. Occupation reinforced gulf between Haitian elite and peasants, consolidated mulatto elite power.

events.title: US Occupation Begins
events.description: After President Vilbrun Guillaume Sam killed by mob, US Marines invaded Haiti, beginning 19-year occupation (1915-1934). US claimed occupation was to restore order, protect American interests and block German influence in Caribbean. Real motivations included: protecting US banks' investments; controlling Haitian customs (revenues for debt repayment); strategic Caribbean control (near Panama Canal); and racist 'civilizing mission'—US believed blacks incapable of self-government. Occupation was completely unilateral, without Haitian consent. US forced Haiti to sign treaty, transferring fiscal and military control to US. US officials took over Haitian government, Haitian president became puppet. This marked loss of Haitian sovereignty and profound national humiliation.

events.title: US Withdrawal
events.description: Under Haitian continued resistance, US domestic criticism, and Franklin Roosevelt's 'Good Neighbor Policy,' US withdrew from Haiti in 1934 (though retained fiscal control until 1941). US left modernized infrastructure and gendarmerie, but also left deep resentment and new power structures. Gendarmerie became major force in Haitian politics, later dictators all came from its officer ranks. After US withdrawal, Haiti regained nominal sovereignty, but political instability continued. However, occupation experience sparked Haitian cultural and intellectual renaissance: négritude movement emerged; Haitian intellectuals like Jean Price-Mars re-evaluated African cultural heritage and vodou; Haitian nationalism strengthened.

events.title: Papa Doc Dictatorship
events.description: François Duvalier established total totalitarian dictatorship. His rule featured: Tontons Macoutes terror—estimated killing 30,000-60,000; personality cult—Duvalier portrayed himself as vodou loa Baron Samedi (death god) incarnation, wearing signature black clothes, hat and glasses; declared himself president-for-life in 1964; suppressed church, intellectuals and any opposition; systematic corruption—embezzling foreign aid and state funds for personal wealth; economic disaster—Haiti sank deeper into poverty; mass emigration—hundreds of thousands Haitians (including most educated elite) fled abroad (mainly US, Canada and Dominican Republic). Despite brutality, Duvalier received US support for being anti-communist (Cold War geopolitical consideration). Duvalier's rule destroyed Haiti's institutions, drained human capital, set country back decades.

events.title: Duvalier Comes to Power
events.description: François Duvalier, nicknamed 'Papa Doc,' elected president with military support. Duvalier was doctor and nationalist intellectual, participated in négritude movement. He promised to represent black majority against mulatto elite, using vodou symbols to build authority. Duvalier quickly transformed from populist politician to brutal dictator. He established personal power system, neutralized military threat, created notorious private militia—Tontons Macoutes (vodou bogeyman figure). These thugs implemented terror rule, killing, torturing and 'disappearing' thousands of opponents. Duvalier's rule opened one of Haiti's darkest periods.

events.title: Baby Doc Dictatorship
events.description: Jean-Claude Duvalier's 15-year rule was slightly milder than father but equally corrupt and incompetent. His rule featured: continued political oppression, though Tontons Macoutes terror somewhat reduced; extreme corruption—Duvalier family accused of stealing $300-800 million; economic disaster—per capita income declined, Haiti became Western Hemisphere's poorest nation; lavish 1980 wedding to wealthy mulatto heiress Michèle Bennett costing $3 million, enraging impoverished population; Catholic Church-government tensions, especially after liberation theology and human rights advocacy rose; 1980s African swine fever crisis—US-led program slaughtered all Haitian native pigs (crucial for peasants), triggering rural economic disaster; continued mass emigration—'boat people' crisis, thousands of Haitians risked small boats fleeing to US.

events.title: Baby Doc Succeeds
events.description: François Duvalier died, his 19-year-old son Jean-Claude Duvalier, nicknamed 'Baby Doc,' succeeded as president-for-life, becoming world's youngest head of state. Constitution amended reducing presidential minimum age from 40 to 18 to legitimize Jean-Claude. This dynastic-style power transfer in modern republic was very rare. Jean-Claude initially controlled by his mother Simone and father's advisors. His rule initially slightly loosened political oppression, but corruption reached new heights. Jean-Claude and his cronies blatantly plundered national wealth, lived lavishly while Haitians sank into deeper poverty.

events.title: Military Dictatorship and Chaos
events.description: After Duvalier's fall, Haiti experienced chaotic transition period ruled by military junta. Period featured: continued political violence and human rights violations; conflicts between former Tontons Macoutes and reformers; multiple coups and government changes; passage of new 1987 constitution establishing democratic framework; November 1987 election day massacre—thugs massacred voters at polling stations, election canceled; manipulated January 1988 election produced military-backed President Leslie Manigat, but he was ousted by coup months later; economy continued deteriorating; international isolation and reduced aid; hopes for democratic transition gradually faded. This period revealed deep problems: lack of democratic culture, military unwilling to relinquish power, elite resistance to real reform.

events.title: Duvalier's Fall
events.description: Facing growing protests, economic collapse and US pressure, Jean-Claude Duvalier fled to France exile (aboard US Air Force plane), ending Duvalier family's 29-year rule. Massive demonstration movement (déchouaj, meaning 'uprooting') swept Haiti, demanding dictatorship end. People took to streets, destroying Duvalier symbols, attacking Tontons Macoutes. Military took over power, forming interim government. Haitians celebrated dictatorship's end, full of democratic hope. However, these hopes quickly dashed as nation descended into new chaos and violence. Duvalier's legacy was devastating: broken institutions, destroyed economy, traumatized society, and deeply entrenched corruption culture.

events.title: Aristide Elected
events.description: Jean-Bertrand Aristide—a radical Catholic liberation theology priest and poor people's rights advocate—elected president in Haiti's first truly free and fair election with overwhelming 67% majority. Aristide's victory shocked Haitian elite and military, who expected moderate candidate to win. Aristide represented 'Lavalas' movement (Creole meaning 'flood' or 'avalanche')—populist wave of impoverished masses demanding social justice and true democracy. His campaign slogan was 'Power to the Poor.' Aristide promised to raise minimum wage, fight corruption, reform military, provide education and healthcare for poor. Haitian poor placed enormous hope in Aristide, viewing him as messianic figure. However, elite, military and business community feared Aristide's radical agenda.

events.title: Military Regime and International Sanctions
events.description: During Cédras military regime, Haiti descended into one of its darkest periods. Estimated 3,000-5,000 civilians killed, many tortured and raped. OAS and UN imposed trade embargo, hoping to force military to surrender power. But sanctions mainly hurt poor, while elite evaded sanctions through smuggling and profited. Tens of thousands Haitians fled by boat to US, triggering humanitarian crisis. US initially repatriated refugees, claiming they were economic not political refugees, drawing human rights groups' criticism. Aristide lobbied in Washington for international support, calling for military intervention to restore democracy. International negotiations tried to reach peaceful resolution, but repeatedly failed, military refused to concede. Violence and poverty intensified, Haiti became international crisis focus.

events.title: Raoul Cédras Coup
events.description: Army Commander Brigadier General Raoul Cédras led military coup overthrowing Aristide. Coup was extremely violent, soldiers and civilians loyal to Aristide killed. Aristide fled to Venezuela, later to US. Cédras established military dictatorship, paramilitary group FRAPH (Front for Advancement and Progress of Haiti) implemented terror, killing thousands of Lavalas supporters. Coup was condemned by international community, OAS and UN imposed trade embargo and sanctions. However, military regime refused to restore democracy, elite generally supported coup. Aristide organized support in exile, appealing to international community to restore his presidency. Coup intensified Haiti crisis, triggering new wave of refugees to US.

events.title: US Intervention and Aristide Restoration
events.description: After diplomatic efforts failed, US President Bill Clinton ordered military intervention. US launched Operation Uphold Democracy, dispatching 20,000 troops preparing for invasion. On invasion eve, former President Jimmy Carter, Senator Sam Nunn and former Joint Chiefs Chairman Colin Powell went to Haiti to negotiate. Facing US invasion threat, Cédras agreed to step down and go into exile. On September 19, US military entered Haiti peacefully without combat. On October 15, Aristide triumphantly returned to Haiti, restoring presidency. Thousands of supporters welcomed him home. However, Aristide had only months left in term (he insisted on completing original five-year term until February 1996), limiting his reform implementation ability. US intervention restored democracy, but also established precedent for foreign intervention in Haitian internal affairs.

events.title: Dissolution of Haitian Military
events.description: Aristide took bold step, dissolving Haitian Armed Forces—the institution that since independence had intervened in politics, launched coups and oppressed civilians. Army replaced by new National Police force, trained with international assistance. This was major turning point in Haitian history: eliminating main coup threat. However, new police force faced challenges: inadequate training, lack of equipment, corruption problems, and infiltration by some former officers and Tontons Macoutes. Dissolving military improved political stability short-term, but also left security vacuum, later filled by gangs and private armed groups. This decision remains controversial: supporters argue it ended military dictatorship threat; critics argue it weakened state's capacity to maintain order.

events.title: René Préval President
events.description: René Préval—Aristide's close ally and former prime minister—elected president in December 1995 election, inaugurated February 1996. This was first time in Haitian history elected president peacefully transferred power to another elected president. Préval faced daunting challenges: rebuilding war and embargo-destroyed economy; implementing IMF-required structural adjustment programs (including privatizing state enterprises); working with stubborn parliament; fighting corruption; improving infrastructure and public services. Préval's term was relatively peaceful but achievements limited. Economic reforms progressed slowly, causing international financial institutions' dissatisfaction. Politics deadlocked, 1997 parliamentary election controversy led Préval to dissolve parliament, ruling by executive decree. Despite many challenges, democratic institutions maintained.

events.title: Contested Elections
events.description: 2000 held parliamentary and local elections, Aristide's Lavalas Party won overwhelming victory. However, elections accused of fraud, especially in method calculating senate seats. Opposition boycotted November presidential election, Aristide reelected with overwhelming majority on low turnout. International community, especially US and EU, questioned election legitimacy, froze aid. This intensified political crisis, opposition refused to recognize Aristide's legitimacy. Haiti again descended into political polarization: Aristide's poor supporters versus increasingly hostile elite and middle class. This election dispute sowed seeds for later crisis.

events.title: Aristide's Second Full Term and Crisis
events.description: Aristide's second full term (2001-2004) descended into increasingly severe crisis. Frozen foreign aid caused economic difficulties; political violence increased, government accused of using armed groups (chimères, meaning 'phantoms') to threaten opposition; corruption allegations continued; human rights situation deteriorated; opposition movement strengthened, called 'Group of 184,' including business, intellectuals and civil society. Early 2004, armed rebellion broke out, former officers and former FRAPH members invaded from Dominican Republic, quickly occupying northern cities. Aristide accused opposition and foreign powers (especially US, France and Canada) of orchestrating coup to overthrow him. Rebels advanced on Port-au-Prince, government forces too weak to resist. International pressure increased, demanding Aristide resign to resolve crisis.

events.title: Transitional Government and UN Peacekeeping
events.description: Transitional government led by Prime Minister Gérard Latortue faced severe challenges: restoring order and security; disarming rebels; organizing new elections; restoring foreign aid; addressing economic difficulties and humanitarian crisis. UN peacekeeping force MINUSTAH deployed about 7,000 peacekeepers and about 2,000 police, mainly from Latin American countries (especially Brazil). Peacekeepers engaged in fierce conflicts with armed groups in Port-au-Prince slums, accused of killing civilians in 'stabilization' operations. Political violence continued, hundreds killed. Many Aristide supporters imprisoned or exiled. Transitional period was highly controversial, criticized as elite coup. However, transitional government successfully organized 2006 elections, despite multiple delays.

events.title: Aristide's Departure
events.description: On early morning of February 29, 2004, as Port-au-Prince was about to be occupied by rebels, Aristide left Haiti for Central African Republic, later exiling to South Africa. Aristide's departure was controversial: US and France said he voluntarily resigned; Aristide insisted he was kidnapped and overthrown by US military, forced onto plane at gunpoint. Truth remains disputed, but clear US was frustrated with Aristide, wanted him gone. After Aristide left, Supreme Court Chief Justice Boniface Alexandre sworn in as interim president. UN Security Council authorized peacekeeping force (MINUSTAH) deployment to stabilize situation. However, violence continued: Aristide supporters clashed with opposition and peacekeepers; rebels and former officers committed reprisals; security deteriorated. This was end of Aristide's political career, but he remained hero or villain (depending on viewpoint) among Haitian poor.

events.title: Préval Reelected
events.description: In February 2006 election, René Préval reelected president, receiving about 51% vote, barely avoiding runoff. Préval viewed as moderate and conciliator, able to bridge gulf between Aristide supporters and opposition. He promised national reconciliation, economic development and improved security. Préval faced enormous challenges: Haiti remained Western Hemisphere's poorest nation, 80% population living below poverty line; unemployment exceeded 70%; infrastructure dilapidated; public services nearly nonexistent; gang violence rampant; political polarization continued; nation highly dependent on foreign aid and diaspora remittances. Préval's second term goal was stability and slow progress, not radical change. He worked to cooperate with all factions, restored relations with Venezuela (obtaining oil subsidies), attracted foreign investment.

events.title: Food Crisis and Riots
events.description: Global food price surge triggered severe Haiti crisis. As food import highly dependent nation, Haiti was particularly vulnerable. Rice prices doubled, many Haitians couldn't afford basic food. In April, 'hunger riots' erupted in Port-au-Prince and other cities, protesters demanding lower food prices. Riots caused several deaths, widespread looting and destruction. Senate voted to dismiss Prime Minister Jacques-Édouard Alexis amid crisis. Crisis highlighted Haiti's extreme vulnerability: dependence on imported food (Haiti once self-sufficient, but imported rice destroyed local agriculture); poor spending 50-60% of income on food; lack of social safety net; government unable to address crisis. International aid increased, but long-term solutions required agricultural reform and economic development, which did not materialize.

events.title: Hurricane Season Disaster
events.description: 2008 hurricane season dealt devastating blow to Haiti. Four consecutive hurricanes and tropical storms (Fay, Gustav, Hanna and Ike) struck Haiti in less than a month, rare disaster. Storms caused about 800 deaths, nearly 1,000 missing, hundreds of thousands displaced. Gonaïves city (also suffered flooding in 2004) submerged in 3 meters of water and mud. Agriculture severely damaged, 70% of crops destroyed. Infrastructure (roads, bridges, schools, hospitals) seriously damaged. Disaster highlighted Haiti's environmental vulnerability: deforestation (forest cover declined from 60% in 1923 to less than 2%) caused soil erosion, landslides and flooding; poor building standards; lack of disaster preparedness; slums built in dangerous areas (riverbeds, steep slopes). International aid poured in, but reconstruction slow and incomplete.

events.title: Election Controversy and Martelly Elected
events.description: Amid post-earthquake chaos, Haiti held presidential and parliamentary elections in November 2010. Elections were chaotic: many voters displaced by earthquake couldn't vote; poor organization; widespread fraud allegations; major candidates (including Aristide's Lavalas Party) excluded. Preliminary results showed government-backed candidate Jude Célestin entering runoff, but popular protests and international pressure (especially OAS observer mission report) led to results being revised, popular musician Michel Martelly (stage name 'Sweet Micky') replacing Célestin in runoff. In March 2011 runoff, Martelly defeated former First Lady Mirlande Manigat. Martelly was political outsider, promising reconstruction, job creation and reform. He gained young people and urban poor support, but also raised concerns for his Duvalierist connections and lack of political experience.

events.title: Devastating Earthquake
events.description: On January 12, 2010 at 4:53 PM, Haiti experienced magnitude 7.0 earthquake, epicenter about 25 km west of Port-au-Prince in Léogâne. This was Haiti's worst earthquake in over 200 years, also one of deadliest natural disasters in modern history. Official estimates had 316,000 deaths (some estimates lower, about 220,000), 300,000 injured, over 1.5 million homeless. About 250,000 residences and 30,000 commercial buildings in Port-au-Prince collapsed or severely damaged. Critical infrastructure destroyed: National Palace, Palace of Justice, Parliament building, most government ministries, major hospitals, port, airport facilities collapsed. UN headquarters collapsed, 102 peacekeepers died including Special Representative Hédi Annabi. Hundreds of thousands sought refuge in makeshift tent camps in Port-au-Prince streets and parks. Earthquake's destruction was so massive because: poor or nonexistent building standards; impoverished construction on steep slopes and fragile soil; extremely high population density; lack of emergency preparedness; weak government capacity.

events.title: Cholera Outbreak
events.description: In October 2010, Haiti experienced cholera outbreak—first in country in a century. Outbreak originated in Artibonite River valley, rapidly spreading nationwide. Scientific evidence indicated cholera was introduced by Nepalese UN peacekeepers, whose camp sewage discharged into river, contaminating water source for millions. UN refused to acknowledge responsibility for years, until 2016 finally admitted 'involvement' in outbreak introduction. By 2019, cholera caused about 10,000 deaths, over 800,000 infections. Outbreak intensified post-earthquake humanitarian crisis, severely damaging trust in international community and UN. Cholera spread rapidly in impoverished Haiti lacking clean water and sanitation. Despite vaccination campaigns and efforts to improve water sanitation, cholera became endemic disease, threatening for years (until cases drastically reduced in 2019). This outbreak was another tragic proof of Haiti's vulnerability, also case of foreign intervention's unintended consequences.

events.title: Post-Earthquake Humanitarian Crisis and Reconstruction
events.description: After earthquake, Haiti faced enormous humanitarian and reconstruction challenges. International community launched one of history's largest relief operations: dozens of countries sent search-and-rescue teams, medical teams and aid supplies; US dispatched thousands of military personnel; hundreds of NGOs poured in. However, relief coordination was chaotic: Port-au-Prince port and airport severely damaged, limiting supplies delivery; roads blocked; communications disrupted; Haitian government nearly paralyzed. Hundreds of thousands lived in tent camps with terrible conditions. In March, donor nations pledged $9.6 billion reconstruction aid at UN conference. But reconstruction was extremely slow and problematic: poor aid coordination; pledged funds slow to arrive; most funds flowed to foreign NGOs and contractors rather than Haitian government or local organizations; corruption; lack of long-term planning; temporary solutions became permanent. Years later, hundreds of thousands still lived in tent camps, rubble clearance incomplete. Earthquake exposed and intensified all Haiti's problems: poverty, weak governance, dependence on foreign aid.

events.title: Duvalier Returns
events.description: On January 16, 2011, Jean-Claude Duvalier suddenly returned to Haiti after 25 years exile, shocking nation. Duvalier claimed he returned to help earthquake reconstruction, but many suspected he tried to use election chaos to return to political stage. Duvalier's return sparked intense reactions: some welcomed him home; human rights organizations demanded prosecution for crimes committed during dictatorship; victims demanded justice. Duvalier was charged with human rights crimes, corruption and embezzlement. Proceedings progressed slowly, obstructed by political interference and weak judicial system. On October 4, 2014, Duvalier died of heart attack in Port-au-Prince, never tried for his crimes. His return and escaping justice highlighted Haiti's culture of impunity and difficulty in holding accountable for past crimes.

events.title: Martelly Presidential Term
events.description: Michel Martelly's presidential term was highly controversial. Achievements included: partial infrastructure reconstruction; building industrial parks to attract foreign investment; improved relations with Dominican Republic; promoted tourism. However, his term also faced severe criticism: tense relations with parliament, long periods without effective government; repeatedly delayed elections, Martelly ruled without parliament by executive decree; corruption allegations, especially involving Venezuelan PetroCaribe fund abuse (billions of aid dollars' whereabouts unknown); human rights issues; authoritarian tendencies. Earthquake reconstruction slow and incomplete, tens of thousands still lived in tent camps. Economic growth limited, most Haitians still lived in extreme poverty. Martelly's attempts to amend constitution to extend term or arrange successor sparked protests. His term should have ended February 2016, but due to delayed elections, successor issue triggered new crisis.

events.title: Aristide Returns
events.description: On March 18, 2011, Jean-Bertrand Aristide returned to Haiti from South Africa after 7 years exile, two days before Martelly's election. Aristide's return also sparked strong reactions: thousands of supporters welcomed him at airport; opposition and international community worried his return would destabilize. Aristide claimed he returned to continue work in education field, not participate in politics. He indeed maintained relatively low profile, but his presence remained political factor. Both former leaders Aristide and Duvalier returning in same year reflected Haiti's political complexity and unresolved historical issues. Neither's return brought reconciliation or justice, but highlighted Haiti society's continued divisions.

events.title: Election Crisis and Moïse Elected
events.description: October 2015 presidential election was plagued by massive fraud allegations, runoff canceled. After reorganizing election, in November 2016, Martelly-backed businessman Jovenel Moïse elected president, inaugurated February 2017. Moïse was agricultural entrepreneur, campaign promised to bring development to rural areas, create jobs, fight corruption. His slogan was 'Haitians feeding Haitians,' emphasizing agricultural self-sufficiency. However, Moïse faced legitimacy questions from start, as election turnout was extremely low (about 20%). He inherited enormous challenges: economic stagnation, high inflation, currency depreciation, widespread unemployment and poverty, dilapidated infrastructure, nearly nonexistent public services, rampant crime and gang violence, political polarization and social distrust.

events.title: PetroCaribe Protests and Crisis
events.description: In July 2018, government announced fuel subsidy elimination, causing sharp price increases, triggering massive violent protests. Protests evolved into broader anti-government movement, demanding President Moïse's resignation, holding PetroCaribe corruption accountable. Haitian Court of Auditors report revealed about $4 billion Venezuelan PetroCaribe funds were massively abused and embezzled, involving multiple former and current officials (including Moïse before becoming president). Protest slogan 'Kote kòb PetroCaribe a?' (Where's PetroCaribe money?) became national cry. During 2018-2019, Haiti experienced wave after wave of protests, strikes, roadblocks and violence. Port-au-Prince nearly paralyzed, economic activity stalled, schools closed, severe shortages (fuel, food, medical supplies). Moïse refused to resign, accusing opposition of attempting coup. Political crisis overlapped with economic crisis (currency plummeting, inflation soaring) and humanitarian crisis (increasing hunger and malnutrition).

events.title: Constitutional Crisis and Authoritarian Rule
events.description: Moïse's term should have ended February 2021 (by 2015 election), but Moïse insisted based on 2017 inauguration date, his term lasted until February 2022. Opposition, legal experts and civil society demanded he step down, but Moïse refused, receiving international community (especially US and UN) support. Moïse used term controversy to consolidate power: June 2020 he dissolved parliament by executive decree and ruled without legislature; early 2021 he appointed new prime minister and cabinet; he pushed controversial constitutional referendum (planning to expand presidential powers); he purged judges and opponents. Critics accused Moïse of establishing dictatorship. Meanwhile, security situation deteriorated: gangs controlled large parts of Port-au-Prince; kidnappings surged (including religious figures and foreigners); massacres frequent; police unable to cope. Economy continued deteriorating, COVID-19 pandemic intensified difficulties. Haiti descended into profound political, economic, security and humanitarian multiple crises.

events.title: Ariel Henry Prime Minister and Gang Crisis
events.description: After assassination, Dr. Ariel Henry appointed prime minister, receiving international community (especially Core Group: US, Canada, France, EU, UN) support. But Henry lacked domestic legitimacy, viewed as foreign-imposed. Haiti descended into unprecedented chaos: gangs controlled over 80% of Port-au-Prince, implementing massive kidnapping, murder, rape and arson; hundreds of thousands displaced, fleeing gang violence; humanitarian crisis worsened—hunger reached emergency levels, cholera resurgence, healthcare system collapsed; economic collapse—currency free fall, inflation out of control, fuel and goods shortages; political paralysis—no parliament, no elections, Henry repeatedly postponed promised elections; international calls to deploy foreign security force, but lacked willing nation to lead. Haiti described as 'failed state,' facing humanitarian, security and state collapse multiple crises.

events.title: President Moïse Assassinated
events.description: On early morning of July 7, 2021 about 1 AM, armed men attacked President Moïse's private residence in Port-au-Prince suburb, shot him dead, and seriously injured First Lady Martine Moïse (she survived and fled to US for treatment). This was first time in Haitian history sitting president assassinated (Dessalines killed in 1806 as emperor). Assassination shocked Haiti and world. Investigation revealed attackers included about 28 mercenaries, mostly retired Colombian military, few Haitian-Americans. Investigation uncovered complex conspiracy involving Haitian businessmen, politicians, security officials and foreign mercenaries. Assassination motive still not fully clear, but related to power struggles, business interests and drug trafficking. Assassination intensified Haiti's chaos: power struggle, three politicians claimed right to lead nation, security deteriorated, international community called for stabilization.

events.title: State Collapse and Transitional Council
events.description: In 2024, Haiti's crisis reached critical point. Gang coalition (led by former elite police officer Jimmy 'Barbecue' Chérizier) launched coordinated attacks, trying to overthrow Henry government, attacking police stations, prisons (releasing thousands of prisoners), airport and port. Port-au-Prince descended into chaos, becoming war zone. Henry stranded abroad unable to return, eventually resigned under international pressure. A Transitional Presidential Council (Conseil Présidentiel de Transition, CPT) composed of Haitian political and civil society representatives formed, goal to restore order and organize elections. In June 2024, Kenya-led Multinational Security Support (MSS) mission began deploying to assist Haitian police against gangs. However, mission was limited in scale, underfunded, with limited effectiveness. Haiti faces existential crisis: state authority nearly completely collapsed; gangs control capital and major cities' majority; millions face starvation; displacement crisis; economic and social structure disintegration. Haiti's future extremely uncertain, international community and Haitian people strive to find path out of abyss. This nation once symbol of freedom and liberation, now becomes synonymous with failure, violence and despair—but Haitian people's resilience and hope persist, awaiting new turning point.
